blocks.x: We're interviewing today in Reserve, Louisiana. That's right, huh?
Yeah, Reserve, Louisiana.
And we're in the back of the New Rhythm Club. Your home is behind us. Let's get your name down, the first thing.
Marsha Lawrence.
That's your full name? Yeah, Marsha Lawrence.
And your name? Marsha Rezheimer.
And I'm Dick Allen. Let's see, what is today's date? Is June the... The 20... I think it's the 28th.
28th, I think. I'm almost sure the 28th.
Anyway, it's Tuesday. We can check in the calendar in a minute. First thing I'd like to know is when you were born and where exactly?
Right here in Reserve, in 1887.
Completely fooled me.
Yeah.
I didn't have any idea. You don't show your age at all? No.
Got to take care of myself. Oh, I see. Do you own this place here? No, I own the fuel home next to the... This is the... Sun-in-law, I own the place. Right there. I see. I used to make caskets and...
I mean, run into the fuel business. I don't do anything like that. I don't work in the fuel home, so... Somebody else doing what's worse. For sure.

Well, back to the music business. How did you get started? Were any of your family musicals that helped you out? No, no one. I started, like I said, the other night, a bunch of boys got together and... started a little band, organized a little band. I don't work in a few months at all. Somebody else doing it for us.
Back to the music business. How did you get started? Were any of your family musicals that helped you out?

No one. Like I said, the other night, a bunch of boys got together and started a little band, organized a little band, and we bought some instruments, and I had an instrument. Like I said, the first day I had my instrument, I could play in tune. From that we began to take lessons from Mr. John Robichaud. He came out here for about six months. Then he discontinued. We had to get somebody else, which we got Mr. Professor Cleven Williams. He stayed about six months with us. Then from that we began to play little jobs with the bands. Gajon Alexander, he was a trumpet player, at least at that time we called it Kone. They had a little band, so he thought I could play pretty good. He asked my daddy, let me play with them. After the dance he'd bring me home. I was about 14 years old. We continued playing for about three years. I played with them. I had seven pieces in the band. I mean cornet, clarinet, drum, we didn't have drum, bass and trombone, and violin myself. We played a while, and then all we were playing was piano score, you know. And everybody could play their parts, it looked like if the one that played the lead would play the melody, and everybody would pitch in. We played that away for about four years, and then we began to get orchestration. And at that time the orchestration were cornet in A and B. You had to switch from A to B, and the clarinet had to have two clarinet, A and B. So we played a good while and the trombone was in triple clef. We played a while and the way, and after a while they stopped writing the music, trombone music in triple clef. So the man played trombone, he had to go back and learn how to read bass clef. And then he did learn. And we played for about maybe ten years. And then the trumpet player, we were playing across the river, at least I didn't go that night, I was sick, and he got droned.
So that's Dajon.

Dajon, Alexander. And at that time the band was named by him, Alexander Right Time Band. And after he got droned, then the way Cromont player and myself, we called it Lawrence and Dewey Arbster. So we played, well I don't remember how many years we played together. And he left the country, so we had another boy to play in his place. And we keep switching off, get some new mans until, then we, until this boy came in with us, Herbert Hall. Well he played the banjo and then after he switched to clarinet. And then we changed the band name again, we called it Nile Band. Called it which? Nile.
Nile. After what?

Well we just, we just called, we just gave it that name. Just made it up. Well the, the Tromont player, the young fellow, he said, well let's change the name. And he gave that name, I think it's an angel name or something like that. So we went by that name for a small good wife, and then the band began to change again. At that time I began to train boys to play. You see, the minute, well Clarence started to play with me, and the minute he could play good, the band from Baden-Rouge would pick him up. I learned to teach a boy to play trumpet. When he could play good, they picked him up. And the saxophone, two of them, they all left.
Could you tell me that full names? Oh yeah.

The one that left, Clarence Hall, the first one left. And then we had one of the French boys playing with us, John of French, he played the trumpet, he left. And after a while, Herbert Trish, played the saxophone, he left. And Roland Arsenault, he left. And Leroy Robinette, he left. And Leroy Robinette, he left. And Leroy Robinette, he left. And Leroy Robinette, he left. What instruments?
Well, Leroy played, Arsenault played trumpet.
And Leroy played the tenor sax. And my boy June, he played, Marshall Lawrence, he played saxophone. And this French boy, I forget it. What relation is he to Morris? His brother. That's his brother.
He played trumpet. So there's several of them that play music in it. Oh yeah, there were four of them.
I think there were four of them playing music. Well I had different boys that played, well a boy by the name of Fredo,
he played with us too, Fredo.

Why the drums? Marzell, he played trumpet with us. He liked. And we had a boy by the name of Lawrence Dewey. He was famous in playing music. Why did he play? He played clarinet. I don't know him. You know him? He's at Lafayette, huh? Yeah, Lafayette. I'm planning to go there and spend a few days with him. Well you'll be sure and tell him how long for this to live. How long for this to live? Yeah. How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? How long for this to live? I'm planning to go there and spend a few days with him.
Well, you'll be sure and tell him hello for me. All right. I'm married from Bro. I guess you know Wilman Bro.
Wilman Bro, I don't think.
He's a bass player. He used to play bass with Duke Collinger. No. And he's from Cross River around Donaldsonville.
Oh, yeah.
I know you'd know him if you saw him.
Oh, yeah. I guess I know him.
He played Madeline and off the trombone, played several instruments. He went out to see Dewey, I believe the last time he was here with my partner, Bill Russell.

Yeah. And then we had that young man, he was a little young boy. I used to have him get a trumpet player from the city. And every time he'd play a few jobs and he'd get a better job, he'd send somebody else. So he brought that fellow Alcorn. I don't remember Alcorn. I know you know him. I can't think of his name. Alcorn. He was a little short chunky fellow. He played a trumpet.
Alvin Alvin.

Alvin, Alvin. Yeah, well I saw him Sunday. Well I sent the boy, my boy, he was going to school again in Yardins. I sent him to get the boy and we were playing a big job at the community club. Someone will see him tomorrow night. I'll tell him hello for you. Yeah? And when he came out and I told the boy, my boy, I said, boy what you brought that boy out here for? I said, that boy can't play. So I said, boy you want to try the music? He said, no, never mind. And I said, well tonight I'm stuck because I had boys that come out, you know, and when they gave them the music, they couldn't play. So, tonight we started playing and put up a piece, he played it. Every piece we put up, they played it. I thought he knew the piece. Everything you put up, they played it. So I got him a few times to play with me. And after that, well, he would play in another band. He was a little boy, a young boy, you know, so small. And then I got a fellow by the name of Joe Johnson. He used to play trumpet too.
What did he play like? Was he an ear man too? Who that?

Joe Johnson. No, no, he used to write music for us. Oh. Joe Johnson, yeah. He's been there for about ten or fifteen years now. And then I got Gardez. Maybe you know him or heard of him. Gardez. He was playing with Joe Robichaud. Not Joe, is it Joe? The young man, Robichaud. The piano player? Yeah.
He's somebody's brother, brother-in-law, we talked with you the other day. What's his?
His brother now played with us. What his brother now played? Saxophone?
I can't remember. I forget. Now you get so many people, you know.
Yeah. Well anyway, Gardez played with us. He played trumpet with us and his brother now played saxophone, but I don't remember his name.
Dajon? His brother-in-law wasn't Harold Dajon, huh?
No, no.
Oh, you know there's so many people.
Myself, I know so many of them. And then we had Poissy, Poissy, Umfries played trumpet with me out here too. He's sick now. He's got a lot of trouble. Yeah? Yeah.

Yeah, he was playing Saturday night, but not Friday night. He couldn't make it Friday night. So sick. No. And then the Eureka band had a parade Sunday and he didn't come on. That's his band now. He's a leader.
And then we had, his name is mentioned on that book. Can't recall his name now.
It's in the book? Yeah, the man- Hold on a second, I'll turn it off. Lewis New Lane.
Yeah, Lewis New Lane. He played trumpet with me. And, well, I had a boy from here play trumpet. He was, he was one of the, kid older trumpet player. We called him Schiff for a short name.
Lewis Matthews. That's his name? Yeah, that's Stonewall's brother. Yeah, you knew of him.

Yeah, well, Poissy and I were talking about that. Yeah, well, he played out here with us a good wife. Before you went to New Orleans? No, after you went to New Orleans. That's when I needed a trumpet player, you see, I was in trouble. Every time I trained a boy to play trumpet, they leave, then I had to begin to get men from this city. And the saxophone too. And Professor Holm played with us trumpet a good wife. From Russia, huh? From Russia. And, well, drums, we had several fellas play drums with us too. Our drum guard, we used to get drums from different places. And then we took a boy with us. And then we picked up a boy, just like they picked me up playing with a band. We picked up a young boy playing drums. He used to be playing on buckets, you know, can, tubs. And I told him, I put him before DeJone, I said, that boy's going to be a drummer. So we picked him up and he played with us a good while until the band from Russia picked him up too. So we had to train another fella. And the one that, on that picture, train him. Well, coming back there was boys that left me. They all came back here and they reorganized. And that's the band we were with. You see, picture you've seen that. And we stayed together until, well, until I stopped playing. Well, I stopped. I used to take engagement for them and I sent my boy, one of my boys, violin player too. So he went out with them until they began to leave again. When did you stop? When did you stop? What year? I stopped since, well, since about, I think about 38. I stopped playing. See, I used to play just for the amusement I get out of it. I didn't make money out of it because I used to, I had a shop and when the bus get out of it, fix it up. When the bus go too big, I'd just forget about it and start over again. And we'd play somewhere and go and eat and I'd buy it and sometimes pay, sometimes forget. I just like the music. Up to now, I still like music.
What kind of music do you like?

I like the music that, what you call them, Lawrence Webb play, you know, music like that. But the other music, that's why I don't fool those boys now. Because for dances, when they give dance for school, I would go with them. But the music they play and you see, I just can't put up with that. You don't like rock and roll? No, I don't like it. I just don't like it. And that's what you have to put it there. I don't like it. I don't find nothing in it myself. I don't know, do they write music for that? I don't believe they do, eh?
I don't think. I think they just stand up and play.

Well, that band I had, the first band I had, the old boys could do that. I mean, anything they hear, they could just go ahead and play. In fact, when we first started, everybody could just, well, Dejon, the man I told you that knew so much music and couldn't explain it, one would play a dance that way, he could just make up a piece and everybody would dance and play it and give it any name. And at that time, we didn't have people that knew anything about music. Anybody that would hear a piece of music, they wouldn't know what it is. They didn't have a grab a phone, they didn't have anything like that. They knew music. You could tell them anything and it was that. In fact, they didn't know how to dance hardly. Especially the white people, they didn't know how to dance at all. And I'm surprised to see how the people that danced now. And music, very few could play music. I mean in the country, you know? I don't remember the city and big places. Well, the only time we would hear music here on the show board would pass. That would be twice in the wintertime, you'd get a show board pass. What show board was that? French and Price. That's the only time we'd see a movie picture. We didn't have nothing like that in the country.
French and Price's show board?

French and, yeah, they would even have a show board pass on the river. You know, they'd stop at the reserve and go across the river. And until they get to New Orleans, they go back. What band would they have on the show? They have a good band. They had a good band. We used to buy music from them.
Do you remember the guys in the band? The name of them?
No, no, no. I don't remember. I don't even know the name. We used to buy music. You know, go around and sometimes they give us a few pieces.
What about Dajon's tunes? Did any of them become popular later? His children? His tunes that he would make up like that.

Well, we never had kept, why don't we keep it up, you know? It would have been alright if we would have brought it, you know? Just play that way until, in fact, most of the pieces that we play... Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
I wanted to ask you about, you told me last time we were here about borrowing the violin from your boss, huh? When you first started.

Oh yeah, when I first started. Well I was learning blacksmith and he had a violin and I bought the violin like today and the next day I told him I could play it. And he said you must be crazy or what? I said you bought it yesterday and you can play it today? I said yeah. So he said, he went home and got his violin and he brought it over the shop. He was living right back. He brought it out and he gave it to me and I couldn't play it. You had to tune it up the right way and I had mine tuned the way I wanted it. So I said well I can't play the way you have it fixed. I didn't know about tuning up. He said I can't play the way. He said well fix it the way you want. So I tuned it up my way and I played for him. So he tuned it up and I kept the sound in my head and went home and I tuned my violin and I played again. And the next day I said well now you can bring it here and I can play it the way you have it. So he brought it and I could play pieces that he used to play. And then he went round to the clubhouse. At that time the people well they were kind of divided a little. You think the people had had the money they had and they had a ballroom they did go to the clubhouse and those that didn't have much money well they didn't go there. So I played and one of the fellows was a violin player so he wanted to send me to school. Wanted me to send me to school but at that time people didn't leave their children to leave that away. So my folks didn't want to leave. So even the work I used to do you know in about six months I could do as much work as he could do. Put up wheels and work a piece of mine and so they told him he said that boy is going to learn how he's going to teach you how to work after a while. And I just kept on that way you see. And well I kept on playing and got up to where I got to be. And I tell you before we left here we used to try to get broadcasts at WWL just to advertise a band you know. And they wouldn't give us a chance there. When we left on that tour, when we got back where everyone played the broadcast and the people here were waiting for us you know. So when we got back we went down to WWL and broadcast and they wanted us every week there. For three or four weeks we went up and tell the boys the hours we had was the kind of back that the boys were waking. We had to be there for four o'clock. We just stopped going. And the funnest thing, the first place we went to broadcast. And we went in the studio and played and we talked we were on the air you know. So the fellas said well you have a nice band. He said put you all on the air tomorrow. And then from that on there we were all played. We had to go.
Where all did you travel on this tour?

I can't recall all. We played, we first played Mississippi, Arkansas, Tennessee, Alabama, Kentucky, Illinois, and Missouri. I think we made 11 and stayed in that tour. From well after we got back where we used to play around in Texas, different places. All the way. New York, Maryland, Northern City, all over.
We really got around.

Oh yeah? We stayed on the road two months and nine days. But every, every, you see right here there was a dancing place. People from all over, New Orleans and Hammond. All over, used to ride at reserve every Saturday night, Sunday night there and dance. And we used to play there. We played there until we got tired. Used to get, they used to get big bands to play there all the time. Did you, you knew Pierron? Pierron played the violin.
I know his trumpet player.
He played violin. Yes.
I met a couple of fellas out of the band. You know? Well, Alvin Alcorn used to play with him some. He played with you.
Now Pierron, was he living at the time? Where's his band? Well he played the violin. Yeah? He hadn't been dead all that long, you know?
But that was after Alvin wrote you. He used to write music. We bought some of his music.
I can't remember. Sister Katie wrote, Mama's Gone Goodbye. Here on, let's see. Blue Orleans Wiggle, I think he did that one.

And that Purple Rose of Cairo is theme song. No. Our theme song was Say a Little Prayer to Me. Was what? Say a Little Prayer for Me. That was our theme song. Oh, I wanted to get some of the early, you know? I didn't know.
I didn't know. It was our theme song. It was our theme song.
It was Say a Little Prayer for Me.
It was our theme song. Oh, I wanted to get some of the early tunes they played, the names of them when you were
first taught them. Do you remember the names of any of them? Oh, I see. It's kind of mixed up there now. Do you remember the first piece you learned?
The first piece I learned was that piece that my old boss used to play all the time. Lizzy on the Rails. I don't remember the real name of it, but that's what they used to call it.
Hiawatha is a real name.
Yeah? I never knew the right name.
I have a record of it. It's pretty jammed. I like that.
Yeah. Watermill and Vine, I think that's one of the numbers we played.
Meet me by the Watermill and Vine, my lending loop?

Uh-huh, and meet the old cherry on the... Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Well, I can remember a piece that we used to play, it was not right after... When I first began to play, Here Come Your Daddy Now. Roby Sho used to play, I remember too. Here Come Your Daddy Now, Oh Pop, Oh Pop, Oh Pop. Or So Mom, or something like that. Uh-huh. We used to play that, uh... Not when I first began, though. It was maybe a little while ago. I'll tell you what, if I can think of some of this. Every once in a while, uh... When I think of a piece that I used to play, I write down the name, you know? And then when I got the name, I can kind of memorize how it goes, and I come back here and practice it. Wait for it.

Well, why don't you write those down and then drop me a postcard next time you're coming to New Orleans, and I'll wait by the telephone at work, you know? I can... Yeah. Just write me that you've come and what time, and when you'll phone me at my work number. Yeah. I'll be up there working, you know?
Mm-hmm.
And the secretary will call me to the phone, you know? Mm-hmm. I wanted to get the name of the people in that picture, too.
Oh, yeah. You got the picture here or the program? No, the picture, I'll get it... I left it over there. I got a program. Uh, let me go get it. I got it in my little shop bag there.
All right, fine. Who booked you on the tour?
Dog Bank from Florence, Alabama. And we have...we didn't know the man, never met him until we got in Alabama. He had a job there and we met him there.
Let's see, here's a picture here, huh?

Yeah, the first one here is Etienne Poissy. He's a trombonist. Trombonist. And this is Roland Arsenault. And this is Charles Louie, drummer. And this is Gelford Dwey, trumpet. And this is myself, Marshall Lawrence, violin. And Edward Hall, bass. Jimmy Reney, banjo. Hubert Trish, saxophone. And clarinet, too, huh? Yeah, all of them played clarinet. Uh-huh. And this is Marshall Lawrence, junior. Saxophone and clarinet. And this is Catherine Osserman, piano. She played the piano. And Leroy Robbin, tenor.
He plays a tenor saxophone.
And they all had clarinet. You see, we had a piece of white heat. Well, they all had to play a...you know they had a part for clarinet.
That picture was taken by the patio, I see. Yeah.

You know, that man used to book us, too. But I can't recall his name. He had a dancing place right on the corner of the rampart. Right by the station. It was two-story building. We took that picture in that place.
Not Banzi.
Huh?
Not Banzi.

Downstairs, they used to sell seafood. And they used to buy fish and oysters. And upstairs, they was dancing places. We took that picture in that place. On Rampart Street. Right. Right by the station.
That couldn't have been Banzi, huh? No. Not Banzi for you.
He used to book different bands. Joe Robichaux and our band and some other bands.
Well, we'll ask Joe Robichaux about it. You don't know.
Uh-huh.

Let's see, your son and Herbert Trist play alto saxophones mostly, huh? Yeah, alto saxophone. And your son's got a soprano sax there, too, huh? Yeah. Uh-huh. Played soprano. You don't see that much anymore. No. No. I think Clarence Hall's still got a soprano, but he doesn't play it. Clarence Hall. Oh, yeah. He doesn't play it much anymore.
He had a, he had a, what did he have? What do you call it, one of those big girls? He had a tenor, he played tenor, I think, Clarence.
He played baritone some now, too.
Yeah, he had baritone, too, I remember, because my son borrowed it from him.
Well, I guess you remember when the Pickwick band played funerals then? Oh, yeah.

Well, I used to play in the brass band myself, lately, you know. I mean, after we had the string band, we used to play all the parades they had. Every society would have a banquet, they would have a brass band to play, to play the parade, and every member of the band that would die would play the parade, you know, for the funeral.
Every member of the band?

Yeah. Any member of any band around the community would die, the band would parade. All the band would get together and play the parade. I mean, play the march, you know. And I told them I didn't want them to play for me, because coming back they played all kind of fast, I don't even like that.
Do they still play the halls up here?
No, they don't. The last one we played was for a man, I forgot to mention his name, he played with me, too. He played bass, Ersk and Tony. He played for his funeral. Ersk and Tony? Uh-huh.
About how long ago was that?

That's been about, what, between eight and ten years? Yeah. Well, what kind of music would the brass bands play? Well, they played mostly Detroit pieces, you know, going to the funeral. But coming back there, they played on Glad You're Dead, Ersk, Ersk, Ersk, Ersk, Ersk, all pieces like that, you know. And just bust it out on the personal levee, coming back from the funeral. I didn't like that idea. On the levee they play?
Yeah, well, they're coming back.
Most of the time, you know, people, they used to play, they walk on the levee, they didn't pass in the low, they, you know, it was cool on the levee, I guess.
Yeah. Well, did they used to play funnels when you were growing up? Oh, yeah, sure. Did they play that kind of writing music?
Coming back, sure, they always did.
Always played that? Uh-huh.
Yeah.
Even when you were a little boy. Yeah.
Do you have any out here who thought about playing music at the funeral?

No, I don't know. I do know that an old man, he used to tell me, he said, why don't you all play, learn how to play child music. He said, after a while, you're going to be playing music for a week. And I said, well, I don't believe that. So, we have a funeral home next door there. And then it came out that we had, we bought a musical instrument to use for fuel, you know, put it on the porch, and then in a funeral home, well, it can sink, let's try pieces, you know, pull that down out again. But just like the old man said it was going to come and start, it was. I guess you all hear that too, maybe, that I'm sitting for a week, you know, they have a, well, it's a phonograph that's playing, you got a lot of speaker, and they play those trade pieces.
But you all never played for a week or anything like that?

No. You mean here? Yeah, we played the trade pieces. Yeah, when it first came out about eight, about eight years ago. And, well, and when they leave, a funeral will leave, they'll put it on, and they'll play until they get to the church.
What kind of musical thing is this? Is this a phonograph?

It's a phonograph that's got a loud speaker. It's in the house. In the house. And what we, we took it out there because people were just in the way, and the people didn't ask for it anymore, and they just stopped using it. And a lot of speakers, in the funeral home now, we have that. All the, all the equipment used to use for that. But the people stopped, well, they stopped asking for it, and they stopped using it. But it was all, or at least we, I don't believe we played it. Many pieces for, if they're awake for Catholics, they don't believe in that. But for the baptism, we used to, or church music, no.
What are some of you, you were talking about playing benefits for the societies. What are some of you?

Well, you know what, every year, every year the society have, they have a mass. They have a mass, and all the members go to the church. And from the hall to the church, they march with the band. They still do that, they don't march in the morning, they come in the truck, you know, they play a few pieces. But at that time, we used to march from here to St. Peter's Church. March and play a few, all different pieces, the right kind of piece all the way, going in and coming back. But, well, we don't have any more brass bands. That's all going on.
So how far, I mean, about is the church from the cemetery, for instance?
From the, well, we have a hall right here. It's about four miles.
And they played the whole way?

Mm-hmm, all the way through. Just like you do for a carnival, you know, just marching. Well, I never did play for carnival, but the brass band Pickwick used to play every year for the carnival. Every year.
What instrument did you play in the brass band yourself?
Alto.
Alto horn, not alto sound?
No, alto horn.
Well, that's not a hard part, huh?
No, no, just compliment. That's all.
Very important, but it's not a hard part.
Yeah, but I don't see why they don't use it.

You take, well, I mean, a school band, we have a school band at the Fifth Ward, and the, the superintendent, and the, well, we, I'm, I'm, well, they say good friend. We, I always do the, all the, the mechanic work, tractors and car, and then I begin to work in school, teaching for the school. Well, he asked me about the band, so I told him, I said, the band is not doing too good. He said, well, what's the trouble? I said, well, the boys that, that have music in him don't have the money to buy an instrument and those that got instrument, they don't have music. So, Mrs. Humphress, uh, Willie's daughter was teaching at the time, Willie Humphress. So, he said, well, what do they need? So, I told him they needed a saxophone again, they needed a tenor, they needed a baritone, different instrument I thought would, would improve the band. So, he said, well, you tell the girl to get ready and you take her down to the wall and go get this instrument. So, we went down and get the instrument, but still they, they don't use all of them. You take the, in a brass band, if you don't have a tenor and a baritone, to me, it's not, it's not a good band without that.
They all have saxophones now.

That's all, that's all they use, saxophone and, well, they have, they have a tuba bass and trombone, two, three trombone, trumpet, and drums. Well, they don't use the tenor. They had an old tenor there, well, I had that repair and I bought a new one.
That's a tenor horn with a band. Yeah, a tenor horn, yeah. Like a brass band.

Yeah, well, that's a nice instrument, they make nice music with the tenor and the baritone. All big bands are still used, but small brass bands, they don't use them, or full bands, they don't use them.
Did all the societies meet at one hall before I forget it?
No, they have different halls, you see, each society. They mostly have their own hall.
And what societies would bury their members?

Well, if one of the members of the Benefisence members died, well, they better remember. What's the name of it? Benefisence, that's the French name. And then they have God Helpers. And they have, well, they have Ease Light. That was all the benevolent society.
Do they have pleasure clubs here, like the Indoorwans, that bury with music?
No, they don't have any pleasure clubs.
Nothing like the Zulus? No. It's all societies.
Society, well, they have pleasure clubs, but they don't bury.
Do the societies pay general expenses instead of it? You mean for the band?

No, the band just play without charging, you know. That's just the way they had, it's just played. They figured out their time coming. And when they're trying to come, the other band, the band members play for them. But it's played out now.
The band only played for musicians at Barrett. Oh, yeah, yeah, just for musicians.
Not for members of the Benefisence? No, no, no, no. Just for the musicians.
Would they ever read any funeral marches?
No. When we played, we had a funeral marches. And I guess the Ornwood too, they had a pretty good band too. Ornwood band. I was a boy when they had a band.
Is Van Son Lashley dead or not?
Yeah, he's dead. He was a good bass player.
Do you know how to spell his name?

SHR NE I think that's the way he was. He was a good reader. He played with our brass band with us too. Our band, you see, we'd make up a brass band for the society, for the band, we wanted to have a parade. He played bass for us. Several times.
Oh, back to those French brothers. You said there were about four of them, Morris.
Morris.
Bob was one of them.
Bob and Johnny. And all of them, three of them.
Johnny with the trumpet.
Yeah. They had a band too. They had a band the same. Well, they left to Edward. They had a band too. They called it the French and White.
French and what?
French and White. The boy played the violin. He used to play with us too. But Bullwide, he played the violin. And Morris played trombone. So they went by that two names, French and White.
Did you know Gus Metcalf?

Oh, I guess so. I knew him, I went to school on him. I went to night school. He couldn't read. You know that man, he could play an instrument and he couldn't read. You know, when we first started, before I started to play with Dijon, well, we asked him to teach us. So he said, all right. And when we get a piece of music, well, we were expecting him to help us divide the music. You know, he said, go ahead and I'll come in. But he couldn't read, you see. He could play anything you play. Anything you hear, he could play. But he couldn't read. That's why I know he couldn't read, you see. We had to play the music for him to play. He played trumpet with us for a while, with our little bands. But he could play any instrument in the band. Gus Metcalf. Yeah, Gus Metcalf.
Well, I heard of him as a trombone player.

Trombone, baritone. That's why I took a liking to that baritone. Baritone, trombone. He didn't play all the instruments in the band though. I mean, he didn't play in the band, but he could play the instruments. Sliding trombone, he used to play a valve trombone. And when that piece, I can't remember that piece came on. That trombone had a part of it. Just then got a slide trombone for him. And the first day he got it, he played. Oh, that man could play in us.
Let's see, there's some like Sally Trombone, and Lasse's trombone, Lowe's trombone. There's a whole family of trombone people. Trombonium is one.
The only two we used was the valve trombone and the slide trombone.
No, I mean, these are the names of the tunes. Oh, they're the, oh. Sally trombone, you don't remember Sally trombone? No. Lasse's trombone, that's still popular. They play that in the circus.

I don't know if it's slide trombone. Something about slide trombone. Well, we played that too after the showboat came out here with that voice. And the Pickwick band liked it so much, so they said, I've got a trombone here, so I've trombone.
I wanted to get the names of some of these fellas straight. We were talking to Kid Thomas' daddy and he mentioned a lot of people.
Well, he used to play in the Pickwick band. Well, Mr. Joe Stewart played the bass, and I know some of the members of the Pickwick band.
What about Nonel Thomas?
Nonel, that's the boy we picked up. That's the boy we picked up playing Marvel to play in our band. Nonel Thomas, that's the boy that we made as drum hunter.
Lionel?

Lionel Thomas. That's the one I told you that he slipped off and went to Baton Rouge. And that's the boy we, you remember I told you I picked up a boy, they picked up a boy in a band just like they did with me, a young boy. I had to bring him home after the dance. You were younger than I was. Yeah, he was a drummer. Lionel Thomas.
I have a hard time understanding Kid Thomas' daddy's pronunciation, you know.
Yeah, that was...

French is hard for me. Yeah. That Petuan, was a musician called Petuan? Petuan? Petuan? He said there was some fella they called Son too, Son Mason or something. I couldn't get it. Either he was a Mason or his name was Mason. Or maybe Son, Son Mason, yeah.
Son. His name was, he played the drum, bass drum. Son Mason. His name was... I don't know how you spell Son. I probably think of his name.
Pierre Mason was his name. Pierre Mason. And he played the bass drum.
And he picked a band. And what about the Auguste brothers? Auguste brothers, yeah. They had one they called... Well, we called him, nicknamed, Peton, but I don't know...
Oh, that's Peton Auguste. He played the...
The bass drum.
The bass drum. And the pickup band. And what about the Auguste brothers?
Auguste brothers, yeah. They had one they called... Well, we called him, nicknamed, Peton, but I don't know...
Oh, that's Peton Auguste.

He played the trombone, the valve trombone. And Auguste, we called him by his family name. Auguste, that's the only... He played clarinet. That's all you called him. And they had one we called Fat. That wasn't his right name. I mean his gift name, but we called him... That was his nickname, you know. Fat, Fat O'Geeze. He used to play trumpet. And they had a young boy, but he didn't play in the band. The young brother, he didn't play in the band. He had a nice start.
What about Ernest Martin?

Ernest Martin, yeah. He played the... He played the alto, the same instrument I played. One the smart. One the smart. And they had the Dejean's brother. We called them Jo Pierre, but his name was Jo Alexander. Dejean's brother. He played the e flat cornet. And the time you used them the e flat cornet the old.
What kind of part was the e flat cornet the old?
You see, I don't know. They played the lead. Play the lead? Up and high? He's like a clarinist. Now, George Stewart, you have his name? Yes. He played the bass. And let's see who else happened.
Did you know George Fisher? Is he in there? Is that his name?
George Fisher?
George something. It may have been Phillips Fisher or something.
No, I remember George Trish. Oh, I see. That boy Herbert played with us there. That's his daddy. He used to play in the honors band.
And what did he play?
I don't know. And his brother played the E flat in the honors band. His brother was Albert Trish. Albert Trish. That was in the honors band. I don't remember him playing, but I knew him.
And who was Murray Cole? What did he play?
Murray Cole. He played the, I think, I think he, Murray Cole, I think he played the drum. That was the honors band. I think he played the drums.
Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Did you know Dave Bartholomew's daddy?
Yeah.
What did he play?
He played the bass. He played the bass. Bass bartholomew. And his name? I don't, not remember exactly. I think his name was Joe. I think his name was Joe.
And who did he play with?

Well, they had a little band my brother played with them. They had a Thomas. I think Thomas started with them. I think he did. If I'm not mistaken. My brother played the violin. And he played the bass. And one of the man in my band played trombone. The same trombone player I have. Blassey. They all younger than I was. They were younger than I was. And then he moved to the city.
Where is Dave from? What town?
Dave from Edgar. I mean, I don't, I don't, I don't, I think he was born in Edgar.
Right across the river.

Right across the river. And he was trying to tell me why he came out. You see, he was working. He would, they sent him out to, he came out to work to help. You see? And he had to work in the field and he came out here. And I don't know how, I got him to start to play with him. He started to come and rehearse with us. And he started to play with me. And he started to play with me. About three years. And then he left to go and play with Sidney. I can't see, but that's Wayne. He played on a boat. He left me to go play with him. And I bought the trumpet he had. I bought it myself to, you know, for him to play. He's a big success now, you know. Yeah, he started to see me, he started to see me every time he passes. Every time. He wants to, he won't forget. He won't forget.
When did he start in with your band? About what year? Do you remember?
I might be there. Some of the parts, somewhere around the 28th. I guess about that time. 28th? About.
And what kind of style was he playing then? Same style he had then. Same style he had then I.

Used to get away from the music all the time. And make his own parts, you know. That's why the trombone player didn't want him. He said, why don't you put that boy out of you? Young boy. I said, well give him a chance. He didn't have music in him. But he'd always get away from that music and add something good.
Did you ever make any records yourself?

No, never have. So I'm sorry we didn't, we never did make any. See? The two things I'm sorry I didn't do is to collect, I applied it from everywhere we played, you know. I think it's a good advertisement for a band. If a band, I try to advise young fellows about that now. Pick up a record and that's all the advertising you need. Just bring it to the man you play and show him what place you played and I know if you play in that place you must be a good man, especially if you repeat the job, play several times. So, there's nothing to do with that.
Could I never see him all that stuff?
Yeah.
Let's see this. Looks like this tape is just about over so maybe we can turn it off. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
A few more things I want to ask you. You want something? Maybe just a little bit. Alright, let's see. I was going to ask you, how many people did you teach? Did you teach a lot of music?
Well, most of them gave them a start, you know. They gave them a start and delicate play. Oh, I guess, in fact, all those that I named, those young fellows there.
You say you helped Kit Thomas' daddy, huh?

Well, that's way after. That's after he stopped playing. I don't count that because it was way after he stopped playing. He liked music and I used to come around. Well, they were the Hall boys. The Herbert Hall. New Earl Robert. The Herbert Hall. And Herbert Trish. And Roland Arcelor. All the boys after they started working. They were getting started music. And after they began to read, then they just went out for themselves. After they moved to the division and then the spell and the lead.
Who sponsored the dances around here? They would put up the money for them. They don't.
Well, we had a community club at Notchua. It was a club they had in response to dancing. And Moray, Louis Moray, he had a dancing place. Every Sunday he had a dance.
What's that Mayflower?
Oh, that was Benevolent Society.
They would have dances?
Yeah, mostly when they had the banquet. Sometime between them they would dance once more. What about the parades? Do you know who put up the money for them?
For the parades, yeah. They would pay for the parades. The Benevolent Society, yeah. They would pay for the parades.
The Parade and dance. Did you play in church once you say you played in church?
Or for the church? We played in church.
I played in church at the University of Dallas. Only for midnight mass around Christmas time. You're a Catholic? Yeah. So I played for the school sometimes since I stopped playing music.
What did the Benevolent Associations do besides have parades and vignets?

Well, they only pay a monthly fee every month and they take care of the sick. They don't pay the doctor bill and pay part of the funeral. All of them. All of them. But they don't have, all of them don't have parades. They don't have parades. I think there were two of them I played this year. With a band. Not walking anymore. They don't have that anymore. No walk? No. You might ride a truck and play a piece in different places.
They have a local band for that? Well, yeah, they have a few bands out here in the country.
They have Lennox and Thomas' brother. He has a band too.
Ken Thomas' band?

No, no, his brother. Oh. He plays mostly in Baden-Ocean. What's that boy's name again, Puro? Thomas' brother, that's Pete boy. Oh, Ballerton. I mean his gift name. Freddie. George Ballerton. George Ballerton. He had the band. He plays badly in Baden-Ocean. Does someone have brass bands out here?
No, no, no.
No, only schools that have, only school bands.
Not even in Donaldsonville or any of the other places that you know of? No.
There's more brass bands. Only schools have brass bands. School. Yeah.
What do the Penabular Associations do at, do they have many things that they, where they just go from play? Do they have bond keys? Yeah, they have bond keys.
They still have bond keys.
Yeah. What does that consist of? How does that work?

Well, they have, a long time ago, when we say a banquet, we'd have the members, and all friends would come around, they would have breakfast and cold drinks, you know, free. But now they cut, most of that cut out, you see. They have to pay for whatever they get. Before that, everything was free. Until that night, the night wasn't charged for the dance. Because now they don't have all that. They might have a fruit, salt drink, you know, the memories? They had a little ice cream with no breakfast or nothing.
So, when one of the members dies, does the whole organization go to the Penabular?
Oh, yeah.
Do they wear any kind of uniforms or anything?

Well, benevolent society, there are some of them, yeah. They have the ladies, anyway, they have the uniforms. What color do you use them? Oh, I don't remember. How do they dress? White and blue, I think. Yeah, white and blue. Now, the Catholic organization, now the Pina Flaherty, well, the ladies dress all in white. And they walk from, well, they don't know how they go. They used to walk from the funeral home to the church, but they all ride now. I think it's been about two years since they walked from the funeral home to the church.
Do they wear a hat of any special gown? No.
For the ladies? Mm-hmm. They have to have, when they go in the church, they have to have something over their head, but no special hat. No special hat.

They don't all wear hats alike in the blood. No. Sometimes in New Orleans, you see them with different little kind of caps and everything. I just wondered if they had the same customs here. I don't know.
Maybe they, maybe they had a, the, uh, what you call it? The Lady Age. Maybe. I don't remember. I don't remember. Well, it's the society, Lady Age. Well,
are there more members in the societies these days than they used to be, or were the societies bigger in the old days or what? No,

they're not as big, it's not big as the old days. Most of the people, it belongs to insurance now. They really want to depend on their society. So, you know, instead of, the, the, the giants are getting short, you see? Because the society doesn't pay as much. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
It's about the same except, well, everything that's coming out new, you know, that's every year something new comes out, otherwise it's about the same.
Well, they have as many dances as they used to?
No, I don't know.
What do you think calls that?
The music box.
I guess television now hurts you a lot. Yeah, yeah. It does. There's so much absolutely free entertainment.

You know, when I first see those music boxes when I was on that tour playing music, I think it was in Chattanooga, we played, I seen they had one in the hall, you know, and I asked them what to do, they used it for dancing. So I thought I didn't really rotate. So that very same night, they had a dance, they had one of those plays that had one of those music box. And that's far from the hall, and they sure didn't really do it. See the people going out, I don't really know how they were going to dance.
Why in the hall they had to play?

They had to play. So when we got back a few years after, we played some big night club in the, between U.I. Berry and Lafayette and during the mission, people started playing music box, you know? They were going out and it's going out and it's all they used to. They were selling a heavy brand on it.
Do you think people spend more money on burial land than they used to? Oh yeah, yeah. They spend a lot more money, but not on music. Huh?

Not on music, no. Just on the other part, huh? Well the music, you know, it's kind of money for them. They're always free, you know, the bands are always free. They're never to charge for the music for a funeral anyway. They were always free.
Well it's cheap in New Orleans, you know, it's, was it 660 a man? There's union scale for a funeral.
To play for a parade? Yeah, that's not much.
No, it's not. Where some of those guys drink, they end up losing money.

Well some of them I guess they do it for the pleasure to get out of it. Not for the money because, I know if they had to play a parade and they have to have a job, they'll pay them better to work than to play the parade. But they just like it. You know, when you like something, you spend money to get that place.
A lot of them like to parade, grow the place. Yeah.

I know, I know, I spend more money playing music than making money. Is that right? Oh yeah. I used to leave, I had a shop, I had four men's work in the shop. Auto mechanical shop. And I used to leave here on Saturday and come back Monday. And at that time you wouldn't get too much money to play. It's $7, $8. Well I could make, I would stay here on Saturday evening and make as much as I could make, playing at night, but I just liked it.
What about when you were just starting, how much did you make?

Two and a half. Two and a half? Two dollars and a half. Well that's a good money. They used to give you a supper, two suppers, when you were good to the place, to eat supper and midnight they'd give you supper. Never had a good price at that time. That's good money for those days, you could buy a lot for two and a half.
Oh yeah.

They paid plenty money for music now, right? Oh what is the date on that photograph? Did I ask you that when that picture was taken? On this? Mm-hmm. Of your band. Tell you one of, when we made that fly, that is one we left, that was in 36.
No, that's the time we made it. And something else I forgot to tell you. You see the last place we played, they gave the name of that place.

We played at Club Pond in Bad Roach. That was the last place we played before we left. And then they gave the band that name, Lawrence Orchestra was Club Pond Orchestra. That's the way they, we went by that name all the way on that tour. And then they just kept it on after we got back.
Well that bass player, his name is Edward Hall? Yeah, Edward Hall. Is he related to Clarence and...
Which one, the one that, this one here, that's one of the brothers. That's one of the brothers.
Yeah. One of the brothers. What did you say Clarence's original instrument was to? Which one, Clarence?
Clarence. Clarence started on the banjo.
And Herbert started on the banjo too.
See when Clarence left, we took Herbert in his place. And he just picked it up and in a little while he could read faster than the uncles.
Edmund told me he had an uncle who played guitar, banjo or something.
Yeah, he had an uncle who played a guitar.
What was his name? I think his name was Edmund.
I think his name was Edmund. He had some sort of nickname. T-Man, we called him. The nickname was T-Man.
Oh. T-Man? Like you said, Little Man.
Little Man, T-Man. Yeah, in French, you know.
That reminds me of something. He played guitar with me too. Oh yeah?

Which band was that? That was right after Dejan, it was Lawrence and Dewey. His brother was playing trombone. I can't recall all of the fellas that played with me. Every once in a while I think of one of them that used to play with me.
That reminds me of that feeling about T-Man. When you were growing up, what was your original language that you spoke? Creole.
Broken French.
And what about people in general? How many of them spoke Creole?

All of them. In this section. You couldn't find a not true family that was reading on here that could speak anything but Creole and French, you know. Some would speak French. What it comes. Some would speak French and most of them would speak Creole.
When did you just start speaking English?
Oh, I have to begin to go out and go to school.
What language did they teach you in school? What language did the teacher talk to?
English.
Yeah.

Talk to English. We learned our catechism like making our first community with the French. Because we didn't go to school. Our lady used to teach all of us. We were on the neighborhood of the writing college. We were all from there and even around the catechism. And we were all from there. And we were all French. Well how many people spoke English around here?

And were there any people who didn't speak English at all is what I'm getting at here? In this neighborhood when you were young. Sure, obviously. Lots of them, huh? Yeah. Lots of them. Yeah. Lots of them. Yeah. Lots of them. Are there still any people who don't speak anything but Creole all around you?
Oh, very few. Very few.
Well today when you're talking around the home what language do you speak?
Me? Well when I talk to my sisters and work I speak Creole most of the time.
What about to your children? Oh.
Yeah. That's nice of them. That's nice of them. Yeah.
Nice of them, huh? Yeah. Nice of them, huh? Yeah. Nice of them, huh? Yeah. Nice of them. Yeah.
Nice of them. Yeah. Nice of them.
They don't know how to speak.
Your children yourself?
They don't understand it but they can't speak it at all. They all went to school and they…
Can that children speak it? Huh? Can that children speak it or understand it? Your grandchildren? No. They can't understand it at all? Most of them do not.
Because people don't use it anymore, see? They don't use it for Creole anymore.
That's the pattern all over the same thing you hear again and again. Yeah. Mm-hm…
Mm-hm… Mm-hm… Mm-hm… Mm-hm… Mm-hm… It was hungry, but most of the time it was hungry.
Occasionally you see it in New Orleans, you know. You see a lot of those ovens as they come up about for us.
How long do they usually wake a person here? One night or longer than that? They have wakes.
Those at wake? If they wake a long hour, no eight hours, but they will always one hour.
At night?
Well, they go a different shift, you know. From morning they wake from 8 to 4, from 12 to 8. Most people wake up to 5.
No, awake when somebody dies. Oh, they wake.

Oh, they're at home. I tell you what, we never let the change of rule. If the family want to stay all night, I stay there all night. And close the place when we leave. And sometimes if you want to stay all night, I just leave them there. We have a place that can go and rest themselves that way. We have a bed and everything. The last week we had that, some of the people stay there all night. They were from Convin and most of the family were from the city. You see, we lived in the city. We had to go back home, we had to be back for the week. So we stayed there and stayed there and through the hall.
Well, you have one room where the body is laid out in, huh? Yeah. And then you have another room somewhere where you could go.
Yeah, we have an office, we have a room that you can go and rest and we have the kitchen where they use for a classroom. And the hall when it wakes the body.
Well, were they served sandwiches with the wake? Yeah. They still do that? Yes, they do that. And did anybody drink with the wake or?

No, no, no. As a rule, when you do their breaks, you usually go to a place. Yeah, a place to see. Yeah, you don't want to drink on with the wake. You want a break of all of your somebody that would come around here with some hearts. And when they're awake, they're going to cut down the music and heart and the music. If they have it, it's very, very normal. I think we're about run out of questions, maybe they're going to answer.
So we'll call it to a halt. We have to get on back. We have to see Thomas' day. We sure do thank you.

segments.title: Opening in Reserve, name, birth in 1887, the fuel and funeral business
segments.summary: Allen sets up the interview at the New Rhythm Club in Reserve, gets names and the date, and Lawrence says he was born in Reserve in 1887 and owns the funeral home next door.

segments.title: Getting started: lessons and playing with Alexander's band at 14
segments.summary: No family musicians; boys bought instruments, took lessons from Robichaud and Cleven Williams, then played with Dejean Alexander's seven-piece band, moving from piano scores to orchestrations.

segments.title: Naming the band: Alexander, Lawrence and Duhe, Nile
segments.summary: The band is renamed as players leave and Herbert Hall joins; Lawrence trains boys who get picked up by Baton Rouge bands.

segments.title: Players who trained with Lawrence and left: Halls, Arsenault, French brothers
segments.summary: Lawrence names former band members and their instruments, including Clarence Hall, Herbert Trish, Roland Arsenault, Leroy, the French brothers, Fredo, Marzell and Lawrence Dewey.

segments.title: Lawrence Dewey in Lafayette and Wilman Bro
segments.summary: Talk of visiting Dewey in Lafayette and whether Lawrence knows bassist Wilman Bro.

segments.title: City trumpet players brought out: Alvin Alcorn and Joe Johnson
segments.summary: Lawrence recalls a young trumpeter who sent replacements, including Alvin Alcorn, who read everything put in front of him, and Joe Johnson, who wrote music for the band.

segments.title: Gardez, his brother, and Percy Humphrey playing in Lawrence's band
segments.summary: Gardez played trumpet and his brother saxophone; Percy Humphrey also played trumpet and is now ill but leads the Eureka band.

segments.title: More trumpeters, a drummer found on buckets, and stopping playing about 1938
segments.summary: Lewis Matthews and others played trumpet; a boy who drummed on buckets was trained, the group reorganized, and Lawrence stopped playing about 1938.

segments.title: Music Lawrence likes and dislikes rock and roll
segments.summary: He plays for amusement, likes the music of bands like Lawrence Welk's and dislikes rock and roll.

segments.title: Early players who made up tunes by ear, and the showboat
segments.summary: Dejean could make up pieces for dances; country people had little music, and the French and Price showboat was where they heard bands and bought music.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: Learning violin from his blacksmith boss, and WWL broadcasts
segments.summary: Lawrence copied his boss's violin tuning and learned to play, then recalls getting broadcasts at WWL after the band returned from its tour.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: The two-month tour and the Reserve dance hall
segments.summary: The band toured several states for two months and nine days; the Reserve dance place drew crowds and big bands every weekend.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: Pierron the violinist and his written tunes
segments.summary: Discussion of violinist Pierron, whose music the band bought, and tunes such as Sister Kate and New Orleans Wiggle.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: The band's theme song and the first tunes Lawrence learned
segments.summary: Lawrence names his theme song, the first piece he learned (Hiawatha), and other early tunes he tries to recall.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: The picture, the program and who booked the tour
segments.summary: Allen asks for names in the band photograph and who booked the tour; Dog Bank of Florence, Alabama, booked them unseen.

segments.chapter: Violin, the 1936 tour and the photo
segments.title: Naming the band members in the photograph and the Rampart Street dance hall
segments.summary: Lawrence identifies each member in the photo, taken at a two-story dance hall on Rampart Street that also booked Joe Robichaux's band.

segments.title: Alto, soprano and baritone saxophones in the band
segments.summary: Talk of which saxophones his son, Herbert Trish and Clarence Hall played.

segments.title: Brass bands at funerals and the music coming back
segments.summary: Bands played for society parades and for deceased band members, with slow pieces going and lively ones coming back along the levee.

segments.title: Funeral home phonograph music replacing bands
segments.summary: Lawrence explains the loudspeaker phonograph used at his funeral home, which people stopped asking for.

segments.title: Society masses, marching to church and playing alto horn
segments.summary: The annual society mass parade to St. Peter's, the Pickwick band at carnival, and Lawrence's alto horn part.

segments.title: The Fifth Ward school band and its instruments
segments.summary: Lawrence helped the school band get tenor and baritone horns, and says saxophones have replaced them.

segments.title: Benevolent societies, burials and unpaid band playing
segments.summary: The societies Benefisence, God Helpers and others bury members; bands played free, and only for musicians.

segments.title: Bassist Van Son Lashley
segments.summary: Lawrence says Lashley was a good reading bass player who played in the society brass band.

segments.title: The French brothers and the French and White band
segments.summary: Morris, Bob and Johnny French had their own band called French and White.

segments.title: Gus Metcalf, who played by ear and could not read
segments.summary: Lawrence recalls Metcalf teaching the early band, playing any instrument by ear, and getting a slide trombone.

segments.title: Pickwick band members and drummer Lionel Thomas
segments.summary: Names from Kid Thomas's father: Joe Stewart on bass in the Pickwick band, and Lionel Thomas, the boy drummer who left for Baton Rouge.

segments.title: Son Mason and the Auguste brothers
segments.summary: Allen and Lawrence sort out Pierre Mason on bass drum and the Auguste brothers' nicknames and instruments.

segments.title: Ernest Martin, Joe Alexander, the Trish family and Murray Cole
segments.summary: Lawrence recalls instruments of other local players, including the Honors band musicians.

segments.title: Dave Bartholomew's father and Dave's three years in Lawrence's band
segments.summary: Lawrence says Bartholomew's father played bass; Dave joined his band around 1928, played his own parts, and left to play on a boat.

segments.title: Never made records; tape change
segments.summary: Lawrence regrets the band never recorded and advises young bands to make records; the tape ends.

segments.title: Teaching young players
segments.summary: Lawrence says he gave most of the young musicians he named their start, including the Hall boys and Herbert Trish.

segments.title: Who sponsored dances and parades, and playing in church
segments.summary: Community clubs, dance halls and the Benevolent Society paid for dances and parades; Lawrence played midnight mass.

segments.title: What benevolent societies do and the bands left in the country
segments.summary: Societies pay dues, care for the sick and bury members; few bands remain, such as Kid Thomas's brother's, and only schools have brass bands.

segments.title: Banquets, uniforms and shrinking societies
segments.summary: Banquets once had free food and dances; societies have dwindled as people turn to insurance.

segments.title: Music boxes, television and the decline of live dancing
segments.summary: Lawrence saw a jukebox replace a band in Chattanooga on tour and says such machines hurt live music.

segments.title: Pay for funerals and dance jobs, and what he earned
segments.summary: Funeral bands play free; Lawrence earned $2.50 when starting and $7-8 later, spending more on music than he made.

segments.title: Date of the photograph and the Club Pond Orchestra name
segments.summary: The tour photo dates to 1936, and the band took the name Club Pond Orchestra from its last stop before leaving.

segments.title: Hall family: Edward, Clarence, Herbert, and uncle T-Man
segments.summary: Edward Hall is one of the brothers; Clarence and Herbert started on banjo, and their uncle T-Man played guitar in the band.

segments.title: Creole and French in Reserve, and English at school
segments.summary: Lawrence grew up speaking Creole; English came with school, and his children and grandchildren no longer understand it.

segments.title: Wakes at the funeral home and closing
segments.summary: Lawrence describes how long wakes last, rooms, food and no drinking; Allen ends the interview.
